title: Brain implant at the University of California, Davis, turns a man's attempted speech into text, and he converses with it at home for nearly two years
summary: A speech neuroprosthesis at the University of California, Davis, decoded Casey Harrell's attempted speech into text, and he used it at home to communicate 1,960,163 words.
account: At the University of California, Davis, a 45-year-old man with amyotrophic lateral sclerosis and severe dysarthria took part in the BrainGate2 trial (NCT00912041). Press identify him as Casey Harrell. The paper reports that before the implant he managed about 6.8 correct words per minute with expert listeners and 6.3 with a head mouse. In July 2023 four 64-electrode arrays were implanted in his left precentral gyrus. From August 2023 a decoder predicted phonemes every 80 milliseconds, and language models with a 125,000-word vocabulary converted his attempted speech to text. The paper gives only the month of the first session. Accuracy was 99.6% with a 50-word vocabulary on day one and 90.2% with the full vocabulary on day two. Prompted-speech accuracy reached 97.5%. Harrell used the system for 248.3 hours of conversation over 8.4 months. Selected conversation sessions had a 3.7% word error rate. On 14 August 2024 Intention to Treat, the podcast of the New England Journal of Medicine, broadcast interviews with Harrell and his wife, Levana Saxon. Saxon said that before the device she was nearly the only person who could understand him. Harrell said that the device lets him converse without a translator and keep working full time. The team's paper appeared in the journal's issue of 15 August 2024. On 12 June 2025 the team reported in Nature that the same arrays drove instantaneous voice synthesis for him, including intonation control and singing short melodies. On 15 June 2026 the team reported in Nature Medicine that over nearly two years he used the system for more than 3,800 hours at home with no researchers present. He communicated 1,960,163 words at an average rate of 56 words per minute and kept full-time employment.
purpose: Built to restore communication by decoding attempted speech from intracortical activity into text. Conversational communication was the intended benefit and is what occurred.
system: UC Davis intracortical speech neuroprosthesis (BrainGate2 trial)
model_version: Four 64-electrode microelectrode arrays (256 electrodes) in the left precentral gyrus; phoneme decoder with an openly available language model assembling phonemes into words and two further open-source language models producing the sentence, over a 125,000-word vocabulary
developer: UC Davis Neuroprosthetics Lab (Brandman, Stavisky) with the BrainGate consortium

ratings.reason: One identifiable person regained conversation with family and colleagues. In the 2026 follow-up the team reports that he used the system for more than 3,800 hours at home without researchers. He communicated nearly two million words and kept working full time.

ai_role.statement: A neural-network decoder (phoneme prediction every 80 ms) combined with language models is the mechanism converting attempted speech into text. The benefit is attributable to the decoding system, with surgery and arrays as enabling hardware.

The UC Davis Health press release reports the same study. The journal's podcast Intention to Treat conducted its own interviews with Harrell and his wife. fields.summary: A speech neuroprosthesis at the University of California, Davis, decoded Casey Harrell's attempted speech into text, and he used it at home to communicate 1,960,163 words.
fields.account: At the University of California, Davis, a 45-year-old man with amyotrophic lateral sclerosis and severe dysarthria took part in the BrainGate2 trial (NCT00912041). Press identify him as Casey Harrell. The paper reports that before the implant he managed about 6.8 correct words per minute with expert listeners and 6.3 with a head mouse. In July 2023 four 64-electrode arrays were implanted in his left precentral gyrus. From August 2023 a decoder predicted phonemes every 80 milliseconds, and language models with a 125,000-word vocabulary converted his attempted speech to text. The paper gives only the month of the first session. Accuracy was 99.6% with a 50-word vocabulary on day one and 90.2% with the full vocabulary on day two. Prompted-speech accuracy reached 97.5%. Harrell used the system for 248.3 hours of conversation over 8.4 months. Selected conversation sessions had a 3.7% word error rate. On 14 August 2024 Intention to Treat, the podcast of the New England Journal of Medicine, broadcast interviews with Harrell and his wife, Levana Saxon. Saxon said that before the device she was nearly the only person who could understand him. Harrell said that the device lets him converse without a translator and keep working full time. The team's paper appeared in the journal's issue of 15 August 2024. On 12 June 2025 the team reported in Nature that the same arrays drove instantaneous voice synthesis for him, including intonation control and singing short melodies. On 15 June 2026 the team reported in Nature Medicine that over nearly two years he used the system for more than 3,800 hours at home with no researchers present. He communicated 1,960,163 words at an average rate of 56 words per minute and kept full-time employment.

produced_by: Preserved speech-motor cortical activity during attempted speech despite severe dysarthria
256-electrode intracortical recording in the ventral precentral gyrus
Phoneme decoder plus large-vocabulary language models calibrated on the participant's own data within minutes
Regulated trial setting (BrainGate2, NCT00912041) with ongoing research support
must_hold: Array signal quality remains stable over months to years
Participant retains the ability to attempt speech and the cognition to operate the system
Decoder recalibration available as neural signals drift
